# How Glial Cells Determine Whether Parkinson’s Aggregates Clear or Propagate
A scientific review in Frontiers in Neuroscience demonstrates that microglia and astrocytes act as a critical functional checkpoint in Parkinson’s disease, determining whether pathogenic alpha-synuclein seeds are eliminated or redistributed across the brain. Authored by Dr R. M. Meade from the University of Bath, the assessment synthesises recent cellular findings to show that non-neuronal cells are neither simple scavengers nor passive casualties.
Instead, the biological outcome of glial involvement depends on a delicate balance between aggregate internalisation, lysosomal processing, and extracellular release. When degradation operates effectively, glia form an efficient sink for extracellular seeds, preventing them from inducing aggregation in neighbouring neurons. However, when degradative pathways become overwhelmed, glia can facilitate the persistence, modification, and transmission of seed-competent assemblies. This perspective reframes glial biology, positioning cellular clearance pathways as central regulators of pathological propagation.
Because microglia and astrocytes surround neuronal synapses and cell bodies, they intercept extracellular fibrils before they reach adjacent neurons. Whether this encounter restricts disease progression or drives further spread depends entirely on whether glial uptake results in complete degradation or incomplete proteolysis that releases active seeds back into the surrounding tissue. Consequently, resolving the intracellular journey of these intercepted fibrils has become a vital objective in neurodegeneration research.

# Immune Cells Found to Cooperate to Fight Toxic Protein Clumps
Immune cells in the brain responsible for breaking down the toxic protein clumps, or aggregates, that lead to nerve cell death in Parkinson’s disease join together to form networks to share the burden, a study showed for the first time.

These networked cells also share energy-producing mitochondria to help neighboring cells stressed by the aggregate breakdown process, the study found.
First, isolated microglial cells exposed to alpha-synuclein clumps ingested the aggregates and triggered inflammation- and cell death-related pathways within the cell. When removed from the aggregate environment, up to 50% of the clumps remained undegraded by microglial cells.
Notably, unexposed (naive) microglia spontaneously joined together with aggregate-exposed cells via tube-like projections making membrane-to-membrane contacts. Over time, the aggregates within cells were transferred and distributed among the unexposed microglia. Even though naive cells formed some contacts, the presence of toxic protein clumps stimulated more microglia-to-microglia connections.
“Together, our data present evidence that microglia have the ability to actively connect to neighboring cells to share the amount of cytotoxic protein accumulations e.g., as a strategy to provide aid and support of protein degradation and to attenuate inflammatory reactions,” the researchers concluded.

“Future studies will have to investigate whether similar contacts and mechanisms exist between microglia and neurons,” they added.

## Abstract
This review examines the mechanisms through which glial cells take up, process, degrade and redistribute extracellular αS seeds. When lysosomal trafficking and degradation are effective, glia can act as a sink for seed-competent αS and restrict neuronal seeding and propagation. In contrast, lysosomal dysfunction, incomplete proteolysis or excessive aggregate burden can promote persistence, modification and redistribution of seed-competent αS, including through extracellular vesicles and intercellular transfer.
## Intracellular fate: degradation versus persistence
### Lysosomal stress can favour release rather than degradation of αS seeds
These findings show that internalisation does not necessarily result in clearance. Uptake is protective only if and when the internalised seed reaches complete degradation. If the processing is incomplete or the lysosomal capacity is compromised, glial cells can retain, modify or release seed-competent αS. The glial lysosome may therefore represent a critical ‘glial checkpoint’ determining whether interception terminates or redirects propagation.

## Abstract
α-synuclein (αS) aggregation and propagation are central features of Parkinson's disease pathology. Preformed fibril (PFF) models have shown that extracellular αS aggregates can enter neurons and seed aggregation of endogenous αS. Within the brain, these seeds also encounter microglia and astrocytes, which efficiently internalise fibrillar αS and can influence its subsequent fate.
## Figures
Glial handling of extracellular α-synuclein seeds as a determinant of pathological propagation. Extracellular α-synuclein (αS) seeds released from neurons can be internalised by microglia and astrocytes and subsequently trafficked through endolysosomal pathways. When lysosomal function is maintained, internalised αS can be efficiently degraded, reducing the extracellular pool of seed-competent material and limiting further neuronal seeding.
In contrast, impaired lysosomal acidification, incomplete proteolysis or insufficient degradative capacity can allow αS to persist and favour its redistribution through extracellular vesicles or direct intercellular transfer. These alternative outcomes define a glial handling checkpoint in which productive clearance limits propagation, whereas non-productive processing can return seed-competent αS to the extracellular environment and promote further spread of pathology.

Scientists tapped the brain’s own cells to clear Parkinson’s plaques! Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine have identified a natural self-cleaning mechanism in the brain that may offer a new way to combat Parkinson’s disease. Working in mouse models that had already developed amyloid plaques and memory problems, the team showed that boosting a protein called Sox9 in astrocytes—star-shaped support cells—made these cells markedly better at engulfing and clearing toxic amyloid-β deposits. Raising Sox9 levels not only reduced plaque burden but also preserved the animals’ ability to recognize familiar objects and environments, suggesting that enhancing astrocyte function can slow or halt cognitive decline even after disease symptoms appear. The study challenges the traditional neuron-centered approach to Parkinson’s therapy by demonstrating that targeting astrocytes and their gene programs could be just as critical as preventing plaque formation in the first place. When Sox9 was removed, plaques accumulated faster and astrocytes became less complex and less active, whereas overexpression had the opposite, protective effect. Although these findings are limited to animal models and further research is needed to understand how Sox9 behaves in the human brain, the work opens a promising avenue for treatments that harness the brain’s own support cells as “vacuum cleaners” to clear pathology and protect cognition. November 20, 2026 Spreading clumps of the protein alpha-synuclein interact with aging to damage support cells in the brain’s substantia nigra and disrupt communication between astrocytes and glutamate-using neurons, according to a study in Molecular Neurodegeneration Advances led by Karin M. Danzer at Ulm University. In a transgenic mouse model of Parkinson’s disease, the team tracked the damage with spatial transcriptomics and single-nucleus RNA sequencing.

Within the brain, these seeds also encounter microglia and astrocytes, which efficiently internalise fibrillar αS and can influence its subsequent fate. This review examines the mechanisms through which glial cells take up, process, degrade and redistribute extracellular αS seeds. When lysosomal trafficking and degradation are effective, glia can act as a sink for seed-competent αS and restrict neuronal seeding and propagation. In contrast, lysosomal dysfunction, incomplete proteolysis or excessive aggregate burden can promote persistence, modification and redistribution of seed-competent αS, including through extracellular vesicles and intercellular transfer. Evidence from microglial and astrocytic models therefore indicates that the outcome of glial uptake depends on the balance between internalisation, intracellular processing and subsequent release. Differences in αS conformation, fibril preparation, inflammatory state, genetic background and experimental model may further explain the apparently protective and pathogenic effects of glia reported across different studies. Understanding the factors that determine whether glial uptake results in productive clearance or continued propagation may identify therapeutic strategies that enhance the removal of pathogenic αS without broadly suppressing glial function.

In Parkinson’s disease (PD), a protein called alpha-synuclein misfolds and clumps together inside brain cells. These clumps are thought to damage neurons over time and can spread from cell to cell, driving the disease forward.

Researchers at the University of Denver and NYU Abu Dhabi — co-led by Sunil Kumar, PhD, a Parkinson's Foundation Stanley Fahn Junior Faculty Awardee — have developed a special molecule called SK-129 that shows promise in blocking alpha-synuclein from clumping and spreading in the brain.

Think of alpha-synuclein clumping like a chain reaction: one misfolded protein causes the next one to misfold, and so on, eventually building up harmful deposits.

Because the SK-129 molecule interacts with important regions of alpha-synuclein, it can latch onto the misfolded protein and prevent it from recruiting others into clumps. Importantly, it targets the toxic, clumped forms of the protein rather than the healthy form, which has normal functions in the brain.

Researchers developed a molecule **called SK-129** that can stop these clumps from forming and spreading — stopping a chain reaction before it starts.

July 23, 2019

## Tracking the spread of Parkinson's proteins from gut to brain

### At a Glance

*   Researchers were able to track the spread of the protein thought to cause Parkinson's disease from the gut to the brain by way of the vagus nerve in mice.
*   Results from the study suggest that finding a way to stop the spread of this protein from gut to brain might help prevent Parkinson's disease in people.

[Brain images of dopamine neurons in mice injected in the gut with misfolded alpha-synuclein (right) and control injected animals (left). Ted Dawson et al. / Neuron, 2019](https://www.nih.gov/sites/default/files/2025-03/20190723-parkinsons.jpg)
The brains of people with Parkinson's disease contain abnormal clumps of proteins called Lewy bodies. These clumps are largely made up of the protein alpha-synuclein, which plays a role in crosstalk between brain cells. Lewy bodies interrupt this communication and are thought to be toxic to certain neurons in the brain.

These neurons produce a chemical called dopamine, which is vital for normal brain functioning. When dopamine-producing neurons start to die, the symptoms of Parkinson's disease emerge. These include shaking, stiffness, and difficulty with walking, balance, and coordination. Some people also experience depression, anxiety, and memory loss. There is no cure for Parkinson's disease, but treatments can provide relief from its symptoms for some time.

Abnormal clusters of alpha-synuclein have also been found in the guts of people with Parkinson's disease. Researchers have proposed that alpha-synuclein may actually first misfold and accumulate in the gut. Recent studies showed that alpha-synuclein clumps can cause nearby normal alpha-synuclein proteins to misfold and form more clumps. These findings suggest that a chain reaction started by misfolded alpha-synuclein could travel from the gut all the way up the vagus nerve, which connects directly to the brain.

2 July 2026

Clumps of sticky alpha-synuclein in brain cells have been linked to the development of Parkinson's. Take a look at the research that's tackling this, to slow or even stop Parkinson's getting worse.

To be able to develop treatments that will slow, stop or reverse Parkinson’s, we need to understand what’s going on in brain cells to cause them to become damaged and die.

As the largest European funder of Parkinson’s research, we’ve been supporting researchers to identify these causes, and translate them into future treatments.

## Could sticky proteins be causing damage?

Proteins perform most of the jobs in our cells. But to function properly, proteins have to be the correct shape and this depends on them folding properly.

In the early 1900s, scientists looking at brain tissue from people who had lived with Parkinson’s under the microscope noticed large clumps present in the cells. In 1997, further research showed that these clumps were made up of a protein called alpha-synuclein, which wasn’t folding properly.

Protein misfolding is common in many brain conditions that get worse over time, including Alzheimer’s and Huntington’s. Misfolded proteins are problematic because they put extra strain on the cell’s recycling system, which works to remove unwanted materials from the cell. They can also start to form protein clumps. These clumps, also known as protein aggregates, can quickly become toxic to cells, making it harder and harder for them to work properly, and eventually causing cell death.

This seems to be what’s happening in Parkinson’s with alpha-synuclein. The sticky proteins form clumps which may play a crucial part in the death of vital brain cells. This makes alpha-synuclein a good target to find treatments that slow down Parkinson’s.

jina.snippet:
Danish researchers have uncovered a toxic mechanism that may lie behind Parkinson’s disease. With a newly developed test platform, they have for the first time shown how clumps of toxic protein can puncture brain cells and drain them of vital substances.

By the time the first trembling hand movement reveals a new case of Parkinson’s disease, the chronic condition has already been active for a long time. Brain cell after brain cell has been attacked and killed. And the “villain” is toxic protein accumulations in the brain cells. That much is well known. The mechanism behind it, however, has until now been unknown. But now, a team of researchers from iNANO at Aarhus University has for the first time shown how some of the protein clumps can kill brain cells by forming holes in them, draining their contents.

Mette Galsgaard Malle hopes she will have the opportunity to follow up on the study in new projects.
“There are some very fundamental things we don’t know about this subject, which I am truly passionate about and would like to explore further. And I believe I can contribute with my biophysical perspective and some slightly different questions than those asked by doctors and molecular biologists in this field of research.”t.”

“We have for the first time shown how some of the toxic protein clumps can attach themselves to the brain cell’s protective membrane and form small pores or holes in the membrane,” explains postdoc Mette Galsgaard Malle, senior author of the study.

The discoveries were made using a new advanced test platform with cell models, which also made it possible to record a video of three of the “cells” under attack.

The research is supported by the Lundbeck Foundation, and the study is published in the renowned journal _ACS Nano_, issued by the American Chemical Society.

keenable.title: Glial handling of alpha-synuclein seeds: uptake, degradation and redistribution in pathological propagation
keenable.snippet: α-synuclein (αS) aggregation and propagation are central features of Parkinson’s disease pathology. Preformed fibril (PFF) models have shown that extracellular αS aggregates can enter neurons and seed aggregation of endogenous αS. Within the brain, these seeds also encounter microglia and astrocytes, which efficiently internalise fibrillar αS and can influence its subsequent fate. This review examines the mechanisms through which glial cells take up, process, degrade and redistribute extracellular αS seeds. When lysosomal trafficking and degradation are effective, glia can act as a sink for seed-competent αS and restrict neuronal seeding and propagation. In contrast, lysosomal dysfunction, incomplete proteolysis or excessive aggregate burden can promote persistence, modification and redistribution of seed-competent αS, including through extracellular vesicles and intercellular transfer. Evidence from microglial and astrocytic models therefore indicates that the outcome of glial uptake depends on the balance between internalisation, intracellular processing and subsequent release. Differences in αS conformation, fibril preparation, inflammatory state, genetic background and experimental model may further explain the apparently protective and pathogenic effects of glia reported across different studies. Understanding the factors that determine whether glial uptake results in productive clearance or continued propagation may identify therapeutic strategies that enhance the removal of pathogenic αS without broadly suppressing glial function.

keenable.title: Brain clearance of protein aggregates in degenerative diseases: the role of microglia and astrocytes
keenable.snippet:
Protein aggregation and impaired clearance constitute central pathological hallmarks of numerous neurodegenera-
tive diseases, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and frontotemporal
dementia. Misfolded proteins, both extracellular and intracellular, disrupt proteostasis and contribute to synaptic
dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and neuronal loss. Within the central nervous system, glial cells serve as the primary
mediators of pathological protein clearance. Microglia detect, phagocytose, and degrade aggregated proteins. How-
ever, under chronic pathological stress, microglial function turns from clearing pathological proteins to paradoxically
facilitating their spread. Astrocytes, which provide metabolic and homeostatic support for neurons, also participate
in the clearance of aggregates through phagocytosis and glymphatic drainage. Critically, crosstalk between astro-
cytes and microglia enhances the clearance: microglia can recruit and process aggregates internalized by astrocytes,
while astrocyte-derived signals modulate the microglial phagocytic activity. Aging, genetic risk factors, or sustained
neuroinflammation may reduce the efficiency of glial removal of aggregates and accelerate disease progression.
Understanding the cellular and molecular underpinnings of microglial and astrocytic clearance pathways is essential
for developing therapies aimed at restoring proteostasis and mitigating neurodegeneration.

keenable.title: How Glial Cells Determine Whether Parkinson's Aggregates Clear or
keenable.snippet:
A scientific review in Frontiers in Neuroscience demonstrates that microglia and astrocytes act as a critical functional checkpoint in Parkinson’s disease, determining whether pathogenic alpha-synuclein seeds are eliminated or redistributed across the brain. Authored by Dr R. M. Meade from the University of Bath, the assessment synthesises recent cellular findings to show that non-neuronal cells are neither simple scavengers nor passive casualties. Instead, the biological outcome of glial involvement depends on a delicate balance between aggregate internalisation, lysosomal processing, and extracellular release. When degradation operates effectively, glia form an efficient sink for extracellular seeds, preventing them from inducing aggregation in neighbouring neurons. However, when degradative pathways become overwhelmed, glia can facilitate the persistence, modification, and transmission of seed-competent assemblies. This perspective reframes glial biology, positioning cellular clearance pathways as central regulators of pathological propagation.
The defining pathology of Parkinson’s disease involves the accumulation of aggregated alpha-synuclein within Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites. Misfolded assemblies act as structural templates that recruit soluble endogenous protein, driving self-propagating inclusion formation. Experimental preformed fibril models have shown that exogenous aggregates enter neurons and induce insoluble, hyperphosphorylated inclusions. In wild-type mice, injected fibrils initiate progressive pathology along anatomically connected circuits, ultimately causing dopaminergic neurodegeneration. Because microglia and astrocytes surround neuronal synapses and cell bodies, they intercept extracellular fibrils before they reach adjacent neurons. Whether this encounter restricts disease progression or drives further spread depends entirely on whether glial uptake results in complete degradation or incomplete proteolysis that releases active seeds back

keenable.title: Intercellular Mitochondrial Transfer in Parkinson’s Disease: Cargo Quality, Cell State Vulnerability, and Therapeutic Selectivity
keenable.snippet:
extrusion pathways influence whether mitochondrial material is retained, degraded, transferred, or released. In acute CNS injury, mitochondrial transfer can restore bioenergetic capacity in stressed cells. In PD, the same process is unlikely to be uniformly protective. PINK1/Parkin, LRRK2, GBA1, and α-synuclein affect mitochondrial quality control, organelle trafficking, vesicle biology, lysosomal clearance, and innate immune activation. These changes create conditions in which transferred cargo may be beneficial, disposable, or harmful. Here, we distinguish direct PD evidence from mechanisms inferred from other CNS disorders and general cell biology. We interpret mitochondrial transfer in PD through two linked variables: cargo quality and recipient cell state. Functional mitochondria may support metabolic repair; damaged organelles may be routed for disposal; and α-synuclein- or mtDNA-associated cargo may propagate proteopathic stress and inflammation. Therapeutic strategies should therefore focus less on increasing mitochondrial movement per se than on enriching competent cargo, preserving donor cell fitness, and preventing transfer routes from amplifying pathology.
### Graphical Abstract
Intercellular mitochondrial transfer in Parkinson’s disease. Astrocytes may donate functional mitochondria to stressed dopaminergic neurons, whereas damaged neuronal mitochondria can be routed toward microglial disposal. In PD, impaired mitochondrial quality control, α-synuclein pathology, mtDNA release, and oxidative stress may shift this process from metabolic support toward inflammatory amplification. When damaged mitochondrial cargo is insufficiently cleared, mtDNA- and α-synuclein-associated material can activate TLR4, cGAS-STING, and NLRP3 signalling in microglia, promoting cytokine release and neuroinflammatory spread. The therapeutic goal is therefore not simply to enhance mitochondrial movement, but to enrich functional cargo and limit pathological transfer.

These diseases include Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), Huntington’s disease (HD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), all of which can lead to a decline in cognitive and/or motor function. A hallmark of many NDs is the accumulation of protein aggregates, such as amyloid beta (Aβ), tau, alpha-synuclein (αSyn), and others.

keenable.title: Glial phagocytic clearance in Parkinson’s disease
keenable.snippet:
An emerging picture suggests that glial cells’ loss of beneficial roles or gain of toxic functions can contribute to
neurodegenerative conditions. Among glial cells, microglia and astrocytes have been shown to play phagocytic
roles by engulfing synapses, apoptotic cells, cell debris, and released toxic proteins. As pathogenic protein
accumulation is a key feature in Parkinson’s disease (PD), compromised phagocytic clearance might participate in
PD pathogenesis. In contrast, enhanced, uncontrolled and potentially toxic glial clearance capacity could contribute
to synaptic degeneration. Here, we summarize the current knowledge of the molecular mechanisms underlying
microglial and astrocytic phagocytosis, focusing on the possible implication of phagocytic dysfunction in neuronal
degeneration. Several endo-lysosomal proteins displaying genetic variants in PD are highly expressed by microglia
and astrocytes. We also present the evidence that lysosomal defects can affect phagocytic clearance and discuss
the therapeutic relevance of restoring or enhancing lysosomal function in PD.

linkup.title: Chaperone proteins may help lower clumps of alpha-synuclein in Parkinson's
linkup.snippet:
Higher levels of proteins called chaperones are linked with lower levels of disease-driving toxic protein clumps in the brains of people with Parkinson’s disease, a new study shows. The findings suggest that increasing chaperone proteins may be a viable therapeutic strategy for Parkinson’s. Data from the study also revealed new evidence suggesting that inflammation within the brain, called neuroinflammation, is a key driver of Parkinson’s. The study, “Single-cell transcriptomic and proteomic analysis of Parkinson’s disease brains,” was published in Science Translational Medicine.
The underlying causes of Parkinson’s disease are poorly understood. One of its molecular hallmarks is toxic clumps of the protein alpha-synuclein that spread through brain cells, which are thought to help drive disease progression.
Neuroinflammation is also a feature of Parkinson’s, but researchers haven’t figured out if inflammation is a cause of the disease or just a consequence of other processes that cause damage in the brain. To better understand the mechanisms driving the disease, researchers analyzed cells in the brains of six deceased people with late-stage Parkinson’s and compared them with six brains from people without the disease.
The researchers compared the findings from Parkinson’s patients with results from studies that performed similar analyses in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease, another neurological disorder. “We wanted to compare the two most common neurodegenerative diseases,” said Le Zhang, PhD, another co-author. Unexpectedly, the data suggested there was little overlap in how nerve cells were affected in the two conditions, even though there were some similarities in how glia, support cells that help nerves to stay healthy and functional, are affected.

linkup.title: Targeting a troublesome protein in Parkinson’s | Parkinson's UK
linkup.snippet:
Clumps of sticky alpha-synuclein in brain cells have been linked to the development of Parkinson's.
In the early 1900s, scientists looking at brain tissue from people who had lived with Parkinson’s under the microscope noticed large clumps present in the cells. In 1997, further research showed that these clumps were made up of a protein called alpha-synuclein, which wasn’t folding properly.  
Protein misfolding is common in many brain conditions that get worse over time, including Alzheimer’s and Huntington’s. Misfolded proteins are problematic because they put extra strain on the cell’s recycling system, which works to remove unwanted materials from the cell. They can also start to form protein clumps. These clumps, also known as protein aggregates, can quickly become toxic to cells, making it harder and harder for them to work properly, and eventually causing cell death.  
This seems to be what’s happening in Parkinson’s with alpha-synuclein. The sticky proteins form clumps which may play a crucial part in the death of vital brain cells. This makes alpha-synuclein a good target to find treatments that slow down Parkinson’s.

Protein aggregation and accumulation are hallmark features of neurodegenerative diseases. Protein misfolding and accumulation defines a prevailing feature of many neurodegenerative disorders, finally resulting in the formation of toxic intra- and extracellular aggregates.

# Brain clearance of protein aggregates: a close-up on astrocytes
## Abstract
Protein misfolding and accumulation defines a prevailing feature of many neurodegenerative disorders, finally resulting in the formation of toxic intra- and extracellular aggregates.
Intracellular aggregates can enter the extracellular space and be subsequently transferred among different cell types, thus spreading between connected brain districts.Although microglia perform a predominant role in the removal of extracellular aggregated proteins, mounting evidence suggests that astrocytes actively contribute to the clearing process.

A scientific review in Frontiers in Neuroscience demonstrates that microglia and astrocytes act as a critical functional checkpoint in Parkinson’s disease, determining whether pathogenic alpha-synuclein seeds are eliminated or redistributed across the brain. Authored by Dr R. M. Meade from the University of Bath, the assessment synthesises recent cellular findings to show that non-neuronal cells are neither simple scavengers nor passive casualties. In a discovery that reframes how scientists understand the brain’s immune response in Parkinson’s disease, researchers at the University of Oxford have shown that microglia, the resident immune cells of the central nervous system, can actively strip toxic protein aggregates out of living neurons without destroying them. The finding, published in Science Translational Medicine and funded by the Medical Research Council and the National Institute for Health and Care Research Biomedical Research Centre in Oxford, reveals a protective mechanism that had gone entirely unnoticed in decades of research into the neurodegenerative disorder. Rather than standing by as dopamine-producing neurons accumulate the misfolded alpha-synuclein protein that defines Parkinson’s pathology, a specialised population of human microglia appears to perform a kind of cellular surgery, carefully excising the harmful material while leaving the neuron itself intact and functional.

The significance of this work lies in the central mystery it helps to address. Parkinson’s disease affects more than ten million people worldwide and is characterised by two intertwined processes: the progressive death of dopamine-producing neurons in a region of the brain called the substantia nigra, and the build-up of abnormal clumps of alpha-synuclein inside nerve cells. These aggregates, known as Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites at later stages, are thought to contribute to neuronal dysfunction and death. For years, therapeutic strategies have sought ways to prevent the formation of these clumps or to clear them once they appear, but the tools of the brain’s own immune system have generally been viewed with ambivalence. Microglia, when persistently activated, are known to release inflammatory signals that can damage neurons, and much of the recent literature has cast them as accomplices in neurodegeneration rather than as protectors.

## This cooperation is impaired in mutations that can cause Parkinson's disease

Microglial cells - (blue: the cell nuclei) can join together using tubular projections (red) to degrade dangerous proteins in a division of labor. Quelle: AG Heneka/University of Bonn

**To break down toxic proteins more quickly, immune cells in the brain can join together to form networks when needed. This is shown by a joint study of the University of Bonn, the German Center for Neurodegenerative Diseases (DZNE) and the Institut François Jacob in France. However, in certain mutations that can cause Parkinson's disease, this cooperation is impaired. The findings are published in the renowned journal Cell.**

The protein alpha-synuclein (abbreviated aSyn) performs important tasks in the nerve cells of the brain. But under certain circumstances, aSyn molecules can clump together and form insoluble aggregates. These damage the neurons; they are for instance typically found in the brains of people suffering from Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia.

The immune cells of the brain, the microglial cells, therefore try to break down and dispose of the aSyn aggregates. seltz.snippet:
There are many things you don’t want gathering in large numbers, including locusts, rioters, and brain proteins. Our nerve cells contain many proteins that typically live in solitude, but occasionally gather in their thousands to form large insoluble clumps. These clumps can be disastrous. They can wreck neurons, preventing them from firing normally and eventually killing them.

Such clumps are the hallmarks of many brain diseases. The neurons of Alzheimer’s patients are riddled with tangles of a protein called tau. Those of Parkinson’s patients contain bundles, or fibrils, of another protein called alpha-synuclein. The fibrils gather into even larger clumps called Lewy bodies.

Now, Laura Volpicelli-Daley from the University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine has confirmed that the alpha-synuclein fibrils can spread. ultimate.title: Glial handling of alpha-synuclein seeds: uptake, degradation and redistribution in pathological propagation
ultimate.snippet: α-synuclein (αS) aggregation and propagation are central features of Parkinson’s disease pathology. Preformed fibril (PFF) models have shown that extracellular αS aggregates can enter neurons and seed aggregation of endogenous αS. Within the brain, these seeds also encounter microglia and astrocytes, which efficiently internalise fibrillar αS and can influence its subsequent fate. This review examines the mechanisms through which glial cells take up, process, degrade and redistribute extracellular αS seeds. When lysosomal trafficking and degradation are effective, glia can act as a sink for seed-competent αS and restrict neuronal seeding and propagation. In contrast, lysosomal dysfunction, incomplete proteolysis or excessive aggregate burden can promote persistence, modification and redistribution of seed-competent αS, including through extracellular vesicles and intercellular transfer. Evidence from microglial and astrocytic models therefore indicates that the outcome of glial uptake depends on the balance between internalisation, intracellular processing and subsequent release. Differences in αS conformation, fibril preparation, inflammatory state, genetic background and experimental model may further explain the apparently protective and pathogenic effects of glia reported across different studies. Understanding the factors that determine whether glial uptake results in productive clearance or continued propagation may identify therapeutic strategies that enhance the removal of pathogenic αS without broadly suppressing glial function.

ultimate.title: Brain clearance of protein aggregates in degenerative diseases: the role of microglia and astrocytes
ultimate.snippet:
Protein aggregation and impaired clearance constitute central pathological hallmarks of numerous neurodegenera-
tive diseases, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and frontotemporal
dementia. Misfolded proteins, both extracellular and intracellular, disrupt proteostasis and contribute to synaptic
dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and neuronal loss. Within the central nervous system, glial cells serve as the primary
mediators of pathological protein clearance. Microglia detect, phagocytose, and degrade aggregated proteins. How-
ever, under chronic pathological stress, microglial function turns from clearing pathological proteins to paradoxically
facilitating their spread. Astrocytes, which provide metabolic and homeostatic support for neurons, also participate
in the clearance of aggregates through phagocytosis and glymphatic drainage. Critically, crosstalk between astro-
cytes and microglia enhances the clearance: microglia can recruit and process aggregates internalized by astrocytes,
while astrocyte-derived signals modulate the microglial phagocytic activity. Aging, genetic risk factors, or sustained
neuroinflammation may reduce the efficiency of glial removal of aggregates and accelerate disease progression.
Understanding the cellular and molecular underpinnings of microglial and astrocytic clearance pathways is essential
for developing therapies aimed at restoring proteostasis and mitigating neurodegeneration.

A scientific review in Frontiers in Neuroscience demonstrates that microglia and astrocytes act as a critical functional checkpoint in Parkinson’s disease, determining whether pathogenic alpha-synuclein seeds are eliminated or redistributed across the brain. Authored by Dr R. M. Meade from the University of Bath, the assessment synthesises recent cellular findings to show that non-neuronal cells are neither simple scavengers nor passive casualties. In acute CNS injury, mitochondrial transfer can restore bioenergetic capacity in stressed cells. In PD, the same process is unlikely to be uniformly protective. PINK1/Parkin, LRRK2, GBA1, and α-synuclein affect mitochondrial quality control, organelle trafficking, vesicle biology, lysosomal clearance, and innate immune activation. These changes create conditions in which transferred cargo may be beneficial, disposable, or harmful. Here, we distinguish direct PD evidence from mechanisms inferred from other CNS disorders and general cell biology. We interpret mitochondrial transfer in PD through two linked variables: cargo quality and recipient cell state. Functional mitochondria may support metabolic repair; damaged organelles may be routed for disposal; and α-synuclein- or mtDNA-associated cargo may propagate proteopathic stress and inflammation. Intercellular mitochondrial transfer in Parkinson’s disease. Astrocytes may donate functional mitochondria to stressed dopaminergic neurons, whereas damaged neuronal mitochondria can be routed toward microglial disposal. In PD, impaired mitochondrial quality control, α-synuclein pathology, mtDNA release, and oxidative stress may shift this process from metabolic support toward inflammatory amplification. When damaged mitochondrial cargo is insufficiently cleared, mtDNA- and α-synuclein-associated material can activate TLR4, cGAS-STING, and NLRP3 signalling in microglia, promoting cytokine release and neuroinflammatory spread.
